title: How do pharmaceutical companies make money, and what matters in a pharma case?
description: Pharma economics for case interviews: R&D pipelines, patents and generics, payers and reimbursement, launch uptake, with a worked patent-cliff example.
hook: Pharma cases are common at life-sciences-focused firms like L.E.K. They have their own logic: years of expensive research, a limited window of patent protection, and customers (doctors, patients and payers) who are not the same people.
body:
How pharma makes money

Developing a drug takes many years and costs a great deal, and most candidates fail in trials. A successful drug earns high margins while its patent protects it. When the patent expires, cheaper generic copies arrive and sales usually fall sharply. This is the patent cliff.

A worked example: the patent cliff

A drug sells £2B a year. When generics launch, if its sales fall 80% within two years, revenue drops to £400M. If that drug is 30% of the company's revenue, the company loses about a quarter of total sales. That is why pipeline strength drives pharma strategy and acquisitions.

Who decides

  • Doctors prescribe.
  • Patients take the drug, and may stop early.
  • Payers (governments, insurers) decide whether to pay for it, and often restrict access.

Many launch problems are really payer problems, not marketing problems.

Typical pharma case questions

  • Why is a new drug selling below forecast?
  • Should we acquire a biotech with a promising drug?
  • How should we prepare for a patent expiry?
  • How should we price a new treatment?

Translate an approval into actual patient sales

A drug is indicated for a disease affecting 200,000 people in a market. Assume 60% are diagnosed, 50% of diagnosed patients meet the drug's eligibility criteria, 40% can access reimbursement, and 25% of that group are prescribed the new treatment. The estimated treated population is 200,000 × 60% × 50% × 40% × 25% = 6,000 patients. At £12,000 net annual revenue per treated patient, that suggests £72 million annualised revenue if patients stay on treatment for a full year. All figures here are fictional practice assumptions.

A candidate who simply multiplies 200,000 by list price would miss diagnosis, treatment eligibility, payer restrictions and prescriber adoption. In addition, net realised price may be lower than list price due to confidential rebates, and revenue depends on actual treatment duration and adherence. A launch forecast should include how quickly physicians adopt the medicine and what happens when competitors enter.

If the interviewer asks why launch sales are below forecast, compare the funnel stage by stage: disease prevalence, diagnosed patients, eligible patients, covered patients, prescriptions and repeat prescriptions. Look for the biggest gap versus plan rather than offering more advertising immediately. Regulatory approval does not necessarily ensure reimbursement or physician acceptance.

For patent-expiry cases, distinguish volume from price: generics or biosimilars may reduce both the originator's unit share and its net price. The right response could involve new indications, differentiated formulations, cost changes or a pipeline investment, but each needs an economic case.
